sections.body:
Appliance symbols are a small international language. A washing machine sold in Hanoi, Madrid or Manila carries the same few dozen pictures, and they mean the same thing in every country. The reason is practical: a machine has to be understood by a person who cannot read the manual, and a picture survives translation while a word does not.

Most of these symbols are not inventions of one brand. They are drawn from international standards, which is why a familiar pictogram appears on machines from different makers in the same position. That is good news for anyone who moves house, travels, or buys a second-hand machine from another country.

The symbols fall into a small number of families. **Control symbols** tell you how to run the machine: power, start, pause, programme selection, delay. **Setting symbols** tell you what to choose: temperature, spin speed, soil level, load type. **Care symbols** tell you what goes in the drawer: salt, detergent, rinse aid. **Status symbols** tell you what the machine is doing: locked door, filter needs cleaning, end of cycle.

Every symbol is small, printed on the panel or moulded into the plastic, and usually printed again in the manual. The manual is the authority, and the panel is the quick reference. When the two seem to disagree, the manual wins, because the panel shows you the shapes and the manual explains them.

Two habits make this easy. First, learn the ten symbols you will actually use, and ignore the rest until you need them. Second, look for the same symbol rather than reading the words next to it. The picture for cotton is the same picture in every country, whether the word beside it says cotton, cotton or Baumwolle.

One warning is worth saying at the start. Symbols are usually moulded in plastic or printed on the fascia, and they wear out. A faded thermometer on a machine in a launderette may be a machine that has been scrubbed clean many times. When a symbol is unclear, check the manual, or check the model number, rather than guessing.
examples: The picture of a filled water bottle means the machine has used its delay start.
I recognise the symbol, but I cannot read the word under it, so I am checking the manual.
sections.heading: Why a washing machine talks in pictures

sections.body:
These are the symbols that appear on almost every washing machine, dishwasher and oven. Learn this short list first and you can operate most machines you will ever meet.

The two you will press every single day are the start and the pause button. Some machines put them in separate places; others use one button for both, and you press it twice to stop.

The power symbol is a circle with a vertical line at the top for on and a plain circle for off. On some machines it is drawn as a single circle with a line through it, and pressing it briefly puts the display to sleep rather than switching the machine off.

The programme selector is a dial with marks around it. On a machine with a screen it may be a row of buttons instead, and the pictures above them are the programmes.

The temperature symbol is a thermometer. The number next to it is the water temperature for the main wash, not the temperature of the finished clothes. A symbol with a small line across the top means cold water, usually 30 °C or below.

The child lock is a padlock. When it is on, the machine will not start until you hold the lock button for a few seconds.

The delay start is a clock face, and it is worth learning because it is the symbol that changes the timing of everything else.
examples: The padlock light is still on, so the door has not unlocked yet.
The triangle starts the cycle and the two bars pause it.
sections.heading: The marks you will meet on any machine

symbols.meaning: Power: a circle with a vertical line means the machine is switched on, and a plain circle means it is switched off.
Start: a triangle inside a circle begins the programme.
Pause: two vertical bars stop the programme so you can open the door. Press start again to carry on.
Programme selector: a dial with programme marks around it, or a row of buttons with a picture above each one.
Delay start: a clock face. You set how many hours later the machine will begin.
Child lock: a padlock. Hold the lock button to release it, so children cannot start a programme.
End of cycle signal: a bell or a speaker. It beeps when the programme is finished.
Door lock: a padlock with a closed door, usually next to a light that stays on while the door is locked.
Temperature: a thermometer with a figure beside it. The figure is the water temperature for the main wash.
Weight sensor: a scale with a weight on it. The machine measures the load and sets the water and the time.

sections.body:
Temperature is the setting that ruins clothes fastest. Wash a wool jumper at 60 °C and it shrinks and felts, and no amount of careful drying brings it back.

The temperature symbol is a thermometer with a number beside it, and the number is the maximum temperature for that programme. It is not a target and it is not the temperature of the drum. It is a ceiling.

Most machines offer the same short range. A filled thermometer with no number means hot, usually 60 to 95 °C. 60 °C is enough for cotton and for heavily soiled linen. 40 °C is the everyday setting for cotton that is not dirty. 30 °C is for synthetics, wool and delicates. A thermometer with a small horizontal line across the top means cold, usually 30 °C or below, and it is the safe setting for anything you are unsure about.

Two rules make this easy in practice. Wash at the highest temperature the care label allows, not the highest the machine offers, because heat is what kills bacteria and it is also what damages fabric. And if a care label says 30 °C, do not use the 40 °C programme in the hope that it will not matter. It will matter, and it will show up as faded colour and shrunken cotton.

Temperature is not only a fabric question. In a dishwasher it is a soil question, and there the numbers run higher, often 55 °C, 65 °C and 75 °C for intensive programmes, because hot water and detergent together do the cleaning that detergent alone cannot. In an oven it is a cooking instruction, and there the numbers are the temperature you set.

A word of caution about the drum: a machine with a temperature symbol that also has a steam or a wash-and-wear mark will heat up at the end of the cycle to steam the load. That is why the door stays locked on some machines after the programme ends. The heat is part of the programme, not a fault.
examples: The care label says 30 °C, so I will use the cold programme.
I am using 60 °C because these are cotton sheets that need a hot wash.
The door is still locked because the machine is doing a hot steam finish.
sections.heading: Reading the temperature symbols

sections.body:
The programme symbols are the pictures around the dial or above the buttons. Each one is a promise about how the drum will move, how hot the water will be, and how long the whole thing takes.

Read the picture, not the number of minutes. Two machines with the same programme name can differ by twenty minutes, because the programmes are tuned to the machine. What does not change is the order of the symbols, and that is what you learn.

The fabrics are the first group. Cotton is the plain, sturdy picture of a shirt or a bucket of water. Synthetics are a shirt with a line through it, meaning the fabric must not be heated hard. Wool is a picture of a ball of wool, and the programme is short, cool and almost still. Delicates are a shirt with a star, meaning very cool water and very little movement.

Then come the purpose programmes. A quick wash is a clock with a short arrow, for lightly soiled laundry that only needs refreshing. A rinse and spin is a bucket with a water drop. A spin only is a circle of arrows. A drum clean is a drum with a brush or a star, and it is the programme you run with the drum empty to clean the machine itself.

And then there are the programmes for bulky and special items: bedding, baby clothes, sportswear, and down or jackets. They exist because a duvet needs more water and a slower spin, and a small baby's clothes need a gentle wash.
examples: I am using the wool programme, because the label says do not tumble dry.
The drum clean programme is the one with the drum picture on it.
sections.heading: The programme symbols on a washing machine

symbols.meaning: Cotton: the everyday programme for cotton, usually at 40 °C with a long wash and a strong spin.
Synthetics: a gentler and cooler programme for man-made fibres, with a slow spin to stop them creasing.
Wool: a short, cool programme with very little drum movement, so the wool does not felt and shrink.
Delicates: the gentlest setting, with low temperature and almost no agitation.
Quick wash: a shorter programme for lightly soiled laundry that only needs refreshing.
Rinse and spin: rinses the load and spins it out, without washing or detergent.
Spin only: empties the drum with a spin, without any washing.
Drum clean: a hot wash with the drum empty, for cleaning the machine itself.
Bedding and duvet: a long programme with extra water and a slow spin for bulky items.
Baby laundry: a gentle, low-temperature programme for small and delicate items.
Sportswear: a programme for technical fabrics that must not be heated too hard.
Down and jackets: an extra rinse and a slow spin for bulky down clothing.

sections.body:
Three settings decide how much water, heat and time a wash uses: the soil level, the spin speed and the programme length. The symbols for them are small, and they are the ones that make the difference between a cheap wash and an expensive one.

The **soil level** symbol shows a pile of dots or soil. One dot is lightly soiled, two is normal, three is heavy. The machine uses this to set the time, and on some machines it also sets the temperature. Washing a lightly soiled load on the heavy setting is one of the most common ways people waste water and electricity without noticing.

The **spin speed** symbol is a circle of arrows. A larger number means the drum turns faster and the clothes come out drier. It also uses more energy and makes more noise, and it can be hard on delicate fabrics. A speed of 1200 rpm is plenty for most clothes. The spin only matters for drying: the clothes come out drier, so the machine spends less time in the dryer afterwards.

Eco mode is usually a small leaf or the word eco on the programme itself. It means less water and less heat for a slightly longer wash. It suits everyday cotton and nothing that is very dirty. On a dishwasher the eco programme is the one to choose every day, because the long, cool cycle cleans well and uses far less energy than a hot intensive cycle.

Delay start, the clock symbol, is the opposite kind of saving. It is not about using less, it is about using it when it is cheaper or when the power is cleaner. If your tariff is cheaper overnight, set a delay start and the machine begins in the night, and you wake up to finished washing.

And **half load** symbols, a drum with half of it filled, tell you the machine to use less water for a smaller load. On some machines the sensor measures the load automatically and does it for you, which is why a modern machine may take longer than you expect on a small load.
examples: It is only lightly soiled, so I am using one dot and the eco programme.
I have set a delay start, so the wash begins at midnight on the cheaper tariff.
I have selected 1200 rpm, so the clothes will need less drying.
sections.heading: Spin, eco and the symbols that change the bill

sections.body:
The last few symbols are the ones that stop a machine working when you do not expect it, and they are worth understanding properly.

The **start and pause** behaviour differs between machines. On many, the start button is a triangle and the pause button is two vertical bars, and the same display shows a small padlock while the door is locked. On others, one button does both: press it once to start, press it again to pause. The label under the button usually says something like start/pause, and that is the label to read first.

The **door lock** is the reason you cannot open the door two minutes into a wash. On most machines the lock is released a minute or two after the programme ends, because the water is hot and the drum is still moving. If the lock does not release, you are not meant to force it. Press pause, wait, and try again.

The **filter cleaning** symbol, a tap or a pump with water, appears on machines that tell you to clean the filter. It is not a fault you caused. A filter that has not been cleaned slows the drain, and the machine will refuse to start a wash rather than overflow. The filter is behind a small flap at the bottom of the front panel, and it is the one piece of maintenance every owner should know about.

The **end of cycle** signal is usually a bell or a short beep, and it can be switched off on some models. If you use the delay start, the beep is the alarm that the wash is finished and needs hanging out, so it is worth leaving on.

Finally, the **on-screen codes**. A letter followed by numbers, such as E1, E2 or F5, is a fault code, and the manual lists what each one means. Look it up rather than guessing, and switch the machine off at the wall before you do anything else.
examples: The door is still locked, so I will wait a minute and try again.
The filter symbol has come on, so I need to clean the filter before the next wash.
The display shows E2, so I am checking the manual for that fault code.
sections.heading: Start, pause and the locked door

sections.body:
The drawer symbols are the ones people get wrong, because the names are unfamiliar and the consequences are quiet. A dishwasher that is never given salt will eventually have hard-water deposits on the heating element and on every glass.

Salt goes in the round cap at the bottom of the tub. The symbol is a salt shaker, or a letter S in some European machines. Salt softens the water so that detergent can work. Dishwashers are designed for soft water, and in a hard-water area they need salt; most manufacturers say to use salt whenever the machine has a salt symbol at all.

Detergent is the powder or the liquid tablet, and it goes in the main compartment of the drawer, the one marked with the letter II or with a flower or a spray. The compartment that looks like a small bucket is for the pre-wash, and only some machines need anything in it.

Rinse aid goes in the wide compartment, marked with a jug and the letter A, or a spray of drops. Rinse aid is not a detergent and it does not clean anything. It makes the water sheet off the glass and the dishes so they dry without water spots.

Softener is the same salt in a different shape. Some machines have a separate water softener setting for the whole machine, and some dishwashers have their own resin softener inside, which is different from the salt cap. If the manual describes a water softener level, that is a setting on the display, not something you pour in.

The **filter** is the last of this family. It sits in the pump at the bottom of the machine, catches the bits of food and the coins, and must be emptied. A machine that will not drain is usually full of coins and grit rather than broken.

The spray arm is the rotating arm below the dishes that throws the water up. If one of its holes is blocked, dishes come out dirty in the same place every time, and the cure is to remove the arm and clear the holes.
sections.heading: Salt, detergent and rinse aid

terms.example: The salt symbol has come on, so I am filling the salt cap.
terms.gloss: Coarse salt that softens the water in a dishwasher so that detergent can work. It goes in the round cap at the bottom of the tub.

terms.example: Put one tablet in the compartment with the two bars.
terms.gloss: The powder or tablet that does the cleaning. It goes in the main compartment of the drawer, marked with two vertical bars.

terms.example: The rinse aid symbol is lit, so I need to top up the wide compartment.
terms.gloss: A liquid added to the wide compartment of the drawer that makes water sheet off the dishes so they dry without spots.

terms.example: A higher spin speed means the washing comes out drier.
terms.gloss: The last stage of a wash, in which the drum turns fast to push water out of the fabric.

terms.example: I am on eco mode, so it will take an hour longer.
terms.gloss: A programme that uses less water and less heat for a slightly longer time. Good for everyday loads, poor for very dirty ones.

terms.example: Hold the padlock button for three seconds to release the child lock.
terms.gloss: A setting that stops the machine starting until you hold the lock button for a few seconds.

sections.body:
You do not need to read the whole manual. You need four answers, and the machine usually gives all four on its panel.

First, find the programme picture you want. The pictures are grouped by type: fabrics on one side, functions on the other. Pick the fabric, then the function.

Second, set the temperature. It is the thermometer, and the number next to it is the ceiling.

Third, set the spin and the soil level. Both are small round symbols and both are optional.

Fourth, look for the three drawer symbols before you start: the detergent compartment, the salt cap and the rinse aid compartment. On a dishwasher this is where most of the mistakes happen, and every one of them leaves a visible mark on the next wash.

Then press the triangle, and check the display shows the programme name and the time. If the display shows a fault code instead, the manual's fault table will tell you what to do in under a minute.

Before the first load, run the drum clean programme on a washing machine, or the rinse-only programme on a dishwasher. It clears out the factory residues and the leftover water, and it tells you straight away whether the machine works.
sections.heading: Working a machine you have never used before

sections.body:
A dishwasher is a washing machine with a different set of programmes, and its symbols follow the same rules. The programmes are chosen by how dirty the dishes are. **Intensive** is the hottest and longest cycle, for pots with baked-on food. **Normal** is the everyday cycle. **Eco** is the long, cool cycle that uses the least energy and is the one to use most often. **Quick** is a short cycle for lightly soiled dishes, and it is a compromise: it uses hot water but does not have time for everything to dry. **Rinse only** is for running the machine when it has been left open or when the drain needs clearing.

The two symbols that cause the most trouble in a dishwasher are the salt and the rinse aid. The salt shaker or the letter S marks the salt cap at the bottom of the tub, and it is what keeps the machine working in hard water. The jug marked with the letter A is the rinse aid, and without it the glasses come out with spots and the plates come out wet.

An oven uses symbols too, and they describe where the heat comes from. The square with a fan inside means the fan oven, which circulates hot air and cooks food evenly, and it is the setting that lets you put a dish on any shelf. A single line at the top of the square means heat from above, for browning and grilling. A single line at the bottom means heat from below, for baking and for putting a dish back under the grill. The zigzag line at the top is the grill, which is strong and direct, and food under it burns quickly, so it needs watching.

The snowflake or the water drop with a line under it is defrost. The bulb is the oven light. And a fan symbol without a square around it starts the fan on its own, which cools the oven faster after cooking and is worth using because the residual heat keeps the kitchen warm.
examples: I am using the eco programme, because it cleans just as well and uses less power.
The grill is on, so I need to watch it closely.
The fan oven means I can put the tray on whichever shelf I like.
sections.heading: Dishwashers and ovens: the symbols that matter most

symbols.meaning: Dishwasher intensive programme: the hottest and longest cycle, for pots with baked-on food.
Dishwasher eco programme: the long, cool cycle with the lowest energy use. The right choice for most days.
Dishwasher normal programme: the everyday cycle for ordinary soiled dishes.
Dishwasher quick programme: a short cycle for lightly soiled dishes, using hot water but little drying time.
Dishwasher rinse only: runs water through the machine without detergent, for clearing the drain or a used machine.
Oven fan: a square with a fan inside, meaning the fan oven that circulates hot air and cooks food evenly.
Grill: a zigzag line at the top of the square, meaning strong heat from above. Food under it burns quickly.
Defrost: a snowflake or a water drop with a line under it, meaning the defrost setting.

item.summary: Washing machines, dishwashers and ovens are labelled in pictures so they can be used in any country. After reading this you can name the common symbols, choose the right programme and temperature, understand the salt, detergent and rinse aid symbols, and work a machine you have never used before.
item.title: Understanding Household Appliance Symbols
